subject: Physics
description: Speed of sound, frequency, pitch, Doppler

questions.stem: The approximate speed of sound in dry air at 20 °C is:
questions.explanation: Sound travels at about 343 m/s in dry air at 20 °C. It is faster in denser media — about 1,480 m/s in water and ~5,000 m/s in iron. 3 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed of light in vacuum. Sound speed increases with temperature (~0.6 m/s per °C) and humidity.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave — it needs a medium (solid, liquid or gas) to propagate. In a vacuum there are no particles to vibrate, so sound cannot travel — this is why the Moon (with no atmosphere) is silent. Sound travels fastest in solids (close molecular packing), slower in liquids, slowest in gases. Light, a transverse EM wave, does not need a medium.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: The pitch of a sound is determined by its:
questions.explanation: Pitch (how 'high' or 'low' a sound seems) is set by frequency — higher frequency → higher pitch. A woman's voice is higher-pitched than a man's because it has more cycles per second (~200 Hz vs ~125 Hz). Amplitude determines loudness. Wavelength is inversely related to frequency (v = fλ) but pitch itself is directly linked to frequency, not wavelength as the controlled variable.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: The human audible range of sound frequencies is approximately:
questions.explanation: The healthy young human ear hears roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz. The upper limit drops with age (presbycusis). Below 20 Hz — infrasound (elephants, whales communicate using it). Above 20 kHz — ultrasound (dogs hear to ~45 kHz, bats to ~120 kHz, dolphins even higher; ultrasound is used in medical imaging, cleaning and in sonar).
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: The apparent change in the frequency of a sound as its source moves towards or away from an observer is called the:
questions.explanation: Doppler effect — the siren of a passing ambulance sounds higher in pitch as it approaches and lower as it recedes. Named after Christian Doppler (1842). Also applies to light: 'red-shift' of receding galaxies (evidence of an expanding universe). Raman effect — inelastic scattering of light. Tyndall effect — scattering of light by colloidal particles. Zeeman effect — splitting of spectral lines in a magnetic field.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: The loudness of a sound is measured in:
questions.explanation: Decibel (dB) is a logarithmic unit — each +10 dB means 10 times the sound intensity, but only about twice as loud subjectively. A normal conversation is ~60 dB, city traffic ~80 dB; continuous exposure above 85 dB damages hearing; 130 dB is the threshold of pain. Hertz measures frequency (pitch). Pascal measures pressure (and sound pressure itself is in Pa, but loudness is expressed in dB).

questions.stem: An echo is heard when the reflecting surface is at least at what minimum distance?
questions.explanation: The human ear needs at least 0.1 s gap to distinguish the echo from the original sound. In that time sound travels 343 × 0.1 ≈ 34 m round-trip, so the reflector must be at least ~17 m (one-way) away. Distances less than 17 m produce reverberation rather than a distinct echo. Caves, deep wells and large auditoriums demonstrate the effect clearly.
